metadata.title: ‘No words’—Machine‐learning classified nonverbal immediacy and its role in connecting teacher self‐efficacy with perceived teaching and student interest

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the German TALIS video study within the international TALIS framework, but the analysis is based on a small, purposefully selected set of recorded mathematics lessons (46 teachers after exclusions) rather than a full nationally representative TALIS student sample. The paper does not report the use of TALIS sampling/student weights or any replicate-weight procedure; therefore, student/sampling weights are treated as not applied or not documented. The multilevel structure (students nested in classrooms) is handled via multilevel modeling, and missing data are addressed using full-information maximum likelihood (FIML), which does not require explicit survey-weight variables. Because the dependent variables are teacher/student survey constructs and an ML-derived nonverbal immediacy score from video, the manuscript does not provide a weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or a weighting strategy for complex survey design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the outcomes are teacher self-efficacy, student-reported enthusiastic teaching, and student interest measured via Likert-type survey scales, plus an ML-derived nonverbal immediacy score from video; the study does not use PV-based cognitive achievement scores. Missing data are handled via full-information maximum likelihood (FIML) in Mplus, which is treated here as a multiple-imputation-style approach for the schema mapping. The paper reports the missing-data method (FIML) but does not provide details on the extent/pattern of missingness, so the exact missingness mechanism cannot be evaluated from the excerpt.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the German TALIS video study mathematics lessons in grades 8–10. From the original 50 teachers, four classrooms were excluded because no video material was available or video quality was insufficient for computer vision analysis, leaving 46 teachers. For NVI model training/validation, video segments were further filtered to those suitable for computer vision (no excessive camera movement; teacher frontal presentation; teacher fully visible; teacher not leaving the frame), yielding 403 30-s segments for training/validation. For subsequent path analyses, NVI was applied to an additional 220 30-s segments from the TALIS video corpus, resulting in NVI data from 623 video segments. The analytic model uses longitudinal pretest (Time 1), post-lesson (Time 3) and follow-up (Time 4) survey measures, with multilevel modeling at the classroom level.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS video study (Germany), mathematics lessons, grades 8–10 (Time 1–4 longitudinal design)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel path model (Model 1 and Model 2): TSESE→NVI was positive and statistically significant (exact coefficient values reported in Table 3 for Model 2: β=0.40, SE=0.20, p=0.048; Model 1: β=0.38, SE=0.18, p=0.034). NVI ML model validation: ICC between algorithm and human ratings for overall NVI on validation data = .690.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS video study (Germany) mathematics lessons the study leveraged teacher self-efficacy (TSESE) and teacher work experience to predict teachers' nonverbal immediacy (NVI) during the lesson (Time 2), finding that higher TSESE was positively and significantly related to higher NVI. This indicates that strengthening teachers’ self-efficacy for student engagement may be associated with more immediate, socially engaging nonverbal classroom communication, though the study is correlational and does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS video study (Germany), mathematics lessons, grades 8–10 (Time 1–4 longitudinal design)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model 2 (sequential effects): Enthusiastic teaching (Time 3)→Student interest (Time 3) was positive and significant (β=0.29, SE=0.12, p=0.021, 95% CI [0.043, 0.529]). Student interest stability: Student interest (Time 1)→Student interest (Time 3) was positive and significant (β=0.67, SE=0.10, p=0.001). Model 1: neither TSESE nor NVI nor enthusiastic teaching were significantly related to student interest at Time 3 when controlling for interest at Time 1.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS video study (Germany) mathematics lessons the study leveraged nonverbal immediacy (NVI), student-reported enthusiastic teaching behaviours, and prior student interest to predict students’ interest after the lesson (Time 3), finding that student-reported enthusiastic teaching behaviours were positively and significantly associated with interest at Time 3 when controlling for prior interest. This indicates that interventions aiming to increase teachers’ observable enthusiasm (as perceived by students) may support immediate boosts in students’ domain-specific interest, while the direct predictive role of ML-classified NVI depends on the model specification.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS video study (Germany), mathematics lessons, grades 8–10 (Time 1–4 longitudinal design)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model 2: Student interest (Time 3)→Student interest (Time 4) was positive and significant (β=0.47, SE=0.15, p=0.002, 95% CI [0.179, 0.767]). Indirect effects were significant: Enthusiastic teaching (Time 3)→Interest (Time 4) via Interest (Time 3) (βind=0.14, SE=0.06, p=0.03, 95% CI [0.01, 0.26]). Model 1: no significant longitudinal effects on interest at Time 4 when controlling for interest at Time 1.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS video study (Germany) mathematics lessons the study leveraged student-reported enthusiastic teaching behaviours, prior student interest, and students’ interest at Time 3 to predict students’ interest 6 weeks later (Time 4), finding that interest at Time 3 was positively and significantly associated with later interest and that enthusiastic teaching had a significant indirect effect through Time 3 interest. This indicates that sustaining students’ immediate post-lesson interest may be a key mechanism for longer-term engagement, while the study suggests that baseline-controlled direct effects may be weak due to high interest stability.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses the German TALIS video study (mathematics lessons in grades 8–10) with 50 teachers and 1140 students, excluding 4 teachers due to missing/insufficient video and using longitudinal surveys at Time 1 (pre), Time 3 (post-lesson), and Time 4 (6-week follow-up). Teachers’ nonverbal immediacy (NVI) during the lesson (Time 2) is computed via a multimodal computer-vision pipeline that trains a neural-network-based model; its validation shows agreement with human ratings (ICC = .690). In multilevel path models, teacher self-efficacy for student engagement (TSESE) is positively related to NVI, and student-perceived enthusiastic teaching behaviours are positively associated with students’ mathematics interest immediately after the lesson (Time 3) when controlling for prior interest (β=0.29, p=0.021). For longer-term interest, Time 3 interest predicts Time 4 (β=0.47, p=0.002), with an indirect effect from enthusiastic teaching via Time 3 interest. Limitations include the small classroom-level sample (46 teachers), lack of reported survey-weight usage, and the fact that the ML component supports measurement of NVI rather than causal identification.
